cards.title: Sharp oracle complexity of approximate monotone inclusion
cards.formal: Determine the optimal worst-case number of exact evaluations of a monotone operator F needed to output u∈U with dist(0,F(u)+N_U(u))≤ε. The 2020 source conjectures (i) Θ(LD/ε) for L-Lipschitz monotone operators and also for the subclass of 1/L-cocoercive operators, and (ii) Θ((L/m) log(LD/ε)) for L-Lipschitz, m-strongly monotone operators. Here U is a nonempty closed convex subset of a finite-dimensional Euclidean space, a solution u*∈U with 0∈F(u*)+N_U(u*) is promised, L,D,ε>0 and 0<m≤L. The source’s algorithms measure distance from a starting point u₀ to a solution, while its oracle lower bounds use a set of diameter D. Its concluding rate statement leaves the precise D convention and joint asymptotic parameter ranges implicit. Those issues remain to be specified, and later results already establish important instances of the proposed rates.
cards.why: Sharp residual complexity would identify the exact cost of obtaining stationarity in variational inequalities and convex–concave optimization, including constrained settings where gap-based guarantees describe a different task.
cards.status_note: Read the primary oracle model and complete conclusion, the 2022 constrained theorem and fixed-point lower-bound statements, and the 2025 strong root-finding theorem. Searches through 12 September 2026 also surfaced stochastic and gap-based variants, which do not replace the deterministic residual task. Important original gaps have been closed; a precise interpretation and current status of the remaining full joint-parameter claim are not certified.

progress.text: Near-optimal bounds and the two restored rate conjectures appear in Section 4.
The general constrained monotone inclusion upper bound reaches O(LD/ε) under the initial-distance convention.
General deterministic fixed-point lower bounds sharpen the earlier restricted-method evidence connected to cocoercive operators.
Strongly monotone unconstrained root finding has the displayed exponential residual guarantee and condition-number rate.

cards.review_note: The recovered two-part conjecture does not specify a joint parameter regime for its Θ bounds, especially the strongly monotone formula as m/L and ε/(LD) vary. The source also uses a feasible-set diameter in its lower bounds and an initial distance to a solution in its upper bounds; the concluding D does not say which class is intended. These choices must be fixed before certifying one uniform minimax statement. Later results settle important versions, so the whole 2020 passage must not be certified as currently open.

importance.reason: A fundamental oracle-complexity question for constrained stationarity and monotone operator problems; existing score retained.

sentences: The task is to make a monotone operator small after allowing a normal vector from the constraint set.
The conjectured query costs are linear in LD/ε without strong monotonicity and logarithmic in accuracy with an L/m condition-number factor under strong monotonicity.
Exact operator evaluations are charged, and residual accuracy is distinct from a weak variational-inequality gap.
Later work supplies the general constrained linear-rate upper bound, sharper fixed-point lower bounds and strong root-finding guarantees.
The source’s distance convention and joint asymptotic regimes still need to be fixed before the whole passage can be certified as one current benchmark.

cards.definitions: The ambient space is R^d with inner product ⟨·,·⟩ and norm ∥·∥₂. For u∈U, N_U(u)={v∈R^d: ⟨v,w−u⟩≤0 for every w∈U}; outside U the normal cone is empty. The required residual is inf_{v∈N_U(u)}∥F(u)+v∥₂. Thus success means that some normal vector cancels F(u) to error at most ε. When U=R^d this reduces to ∥F(u)∥₂≤ε. For all u,w∈U, monotonicity means ⟨F(u)−F(w),u−w⟩≥0; L-Lipschitz continuity means ∥F(u)−F(w)∥₂≤L∥u−w∥₂; 1/L-cocoercivity means ⟨F(u)−F(w),u−w⟩≥∥F(u)−F(w)∥₂²/L; and m-strong monotonicity means ⟨F(u)−F(w),u−w⟩≥m∥u−w∥₂². Cocoercivity implies monotonicity and L-Lipschitz continuity. The source’s deterministic oracle model lets an algorithm adaptively choose a query in U from prior exact values of F and global problem data, including U and regularity parameters; a query returns the whole vector F(u). Only calls to F are charged. Exact real arithmetic and projection onto U are part of the setting, rather than a bit-complexity or membership-oracle problem. Exact computation of the resolvent of F+N_U is not a free call to F. Lower bounds are in sufficiently large dimension; the requested dimension-independent rates are not assertions of the same difficulty in every fixed d. The diameter is sup_{u,w∈U}∥u−w∥₂. An initial-distance bound ∥u₀−u*∥₂≤D can instead hold for an unbounded U; these describe different instance classes. Θ requests upper and lower bounds up to constants, whose uniformity in L,m,D,ε must be fixed. A small weak variational-inequality gap or distance to a solution is not itself the residual guarantee.
cards.answer_criterion: For a specified distance/diameter convention and parameter regime, prove matching worst-case upper and lower oracle bounds for each stated operator class, or refute a proposed rate for that same class and regime. Algorithms must guarantee the normal-cone residual, and lower bounds must apply to the specified deterministic evaluation oracle in sufficiently large dimension. The present record does not certify a complete joint-parameter acceptance predicate. Bounds using exact resolvents as unit-cost queries, or only a weak variational-inequality gap, do not settle it.

context_blocks.title: Residual accuracy is the central distinction
context_blocks.text: Exact monotone inclusion is equivalent to a variational inequality under the source’s assumptions, but approximate versions use different errors. The inclusion residual gives a meaningful stationarity guarantee even when a global gap over an unbounded feasible set is infinite.

context_blocks.title: What was open in 2020
context_blocks.text: The paper gave nearly optimal deterministic evaluation bounds and conjectured removal of the remaining logarithmic gaps. Its parameter-free algorithms are stronger in their lack of advance regularity knowledge than what the Appendix’s general lower-bound oracle requires.

context_blocks.title: The general constrained upper bound is now available
context_blocks.text: Cai, Oikonomou and Zheng’s 2022 manuscript proves O(L∥u₀−u*∥₂/T) normal-cone residual after T iterations for monotone L-Lipschitz F on an arbitrary closed convex U, using evaluations and projections. Thus the missing logarithm in the first general upper bound is not still an open target.

context_blocks.title: Sharper lower bounds and a different oracle
context_blocks.text: Park and Ryu establish sharp fixed-point residual bounds for general deterministic methods. Nonexpansive fixed-point evaluation is connected to cocoercive root finding, but their separate proximal-point results charge resolvent evaluations. A resolvent lower bound cannot simply be relabeled as the F-evaluation complexity of every constrained inclusion.

context_blocks.title: Strong monotonicity has later rate guarantees
context_blocks.text: Yoon and Ryu’s 2025 journal paper gives a strongly monotone Lipschitz root-finding method with an exponential residual rate. Its discussion recovers order (L/m) log(L∥u₀−u*∥₂/ε) evaluations in the ill-conditioned regime. This is a single-valued unconstrained root problem; it does not by itself verify every uniform constrained minimax interpretation of the original two-part conjecture.

cards.context:
Exact monotone inclusion is equivalent to a variational inequality under the source’s assumptions, but approximate versions use different errors. The inclusion residual gives a meaningful stationarity guarantee even when a global gap over an unbounded feasible set is infinite.

The paper gave nearly optimal deterministic evaluation bounds and conjectured removal of the remaining logarithmic gaps. Its parameter-free algorithms are stronger in their lack of advance regularity knowledge than what the Appendix’s general lower-bound oracle requires.

Cai, Oikonomou and Zheng’s 2022 manuscript proves O(L∥u₀−u*∥₂/T) normal-cone residual after T iterations for monotone L-Lipschitz F on an arbitrary closed convex U, using evaluations and projections. Thus the missing logarithm in the first general upper bound is not still an open target.

Park and Ryu establish sharp fixed-point residual bounds for general deterministic methods. Nonexpansive fixed-point evaluation is connected to cocoercive root finding, but their separate proximal-point results charge resolvent evaluations. A resolvent lower bound cannot simply be relabeled as the F-evaluation complexity of every constrained inclusion.

Yoon and Ryu’s 2025 journal paper gives a strongly monotone Lipschitz root-finding method with an exponential residual rate. Its discussion recovers order (L/m) log(L∥u₀−u*∥₂/ε) evaluations in the ill-conditioned regime. This is a single-valued unconstrained root problem; it does not by itself verify every uniform constrained minimax interpretation of the original two-part conjecture.

meta.status_scope: No claim of exhaustive open-status verification
methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. We aim for benchmarks of 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. All three use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The possible 1,000-problem expansion has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Deleted records are absent from the catalogue and exports. Their stable IDs and reasons are retained to prevent reimport. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The targets are 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. Top 100, Top 500 and the possible Top 1000 use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Records marked resolved are placed after the remaining candidates, without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.
